title: Main-Sequence Lifetimes
short: A star's lifetime goes as its fuel over its luminosity, about M^(−2.5), so massive stars die young.
trouble: Students think big stars last longer because they have more fuel.

blocks.html: You estimated the Sun's lifetime as fuel divided by the rate of use. Binary stars showed how luminosity depends on mass. Put the two together, and you can predict how long any main-sequence star will last.

A star's fuel is proportional to its mass $M$ (each burns about the same fraction of its hydrogen on the main sequence). The rate it uses fuel is its luminosity, which grows steeply with mass: roughly $L \propto M^{3.5}$. So the lifetime goes as $$t \propto \frac{M}{L} \propto \frac{M}{M^{3.5}} = M^{-2.5}.$$ Scaling to the Sun's 10 billion years: $t \approx 10\ \text{billion years} \times M^{-2.5}$ (with $M$ in solar masses). A heavier star has more fuel, but its stronger gravity squeezes its core hotter and denser, and fusion speeds up far more than the fuel supply grows.

Main-sequence lifetime $\approx 10\ \text{billion years} \times \dfrac{M}{L} \approx 10\ \text{billion years} \times M^{-2.5}$. Massive stars live fast and die young; small stars last for hundreds of billions of years.

blocks.title: Fuel over rate
blocks.q: A star has $3$ solar masses and $81$ solar luminosities. Estimate its lifetime.

blocks.html: It seems logical that a big star, with more fuel, would last longer. But it burns that fuel thousands of times faster. A $10\,M_\odot$ star has 10 times the Sun's fuel and about 3000 times its luminosity, so it lasts about $\frac{10}{3000}$ of the Sun's lifetime: some 30 million years. Check: every red dwarf ever born is still shining, because none has had time to run out.
